questions.question_text: According to Newton's second law as used in this chapter, how is the net force on an object related to its mass and acceleration?

options.A: Force equals mass divided by acceleration
options.B: Force equals mass times acceleration
options.C: Force equals mass plus acceleration
options.D: Force equals acceleration divided by mass

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes electric charge as introduced in this chapter?

options.A: Charge can take any continuous value, not just multiples of a fixed unit
options.B: Charge is only ever positive, never negative
options.C: Charge is created and destroyed continuously as carriers move
options.D: Charge is quantized in integer multiples of the elementary charge, e = 1.602x10^-19 C

questions.question_text: How is electric potential (voltage) defined in this chapter?

options.A: Potential energy per unit charge
options.B: Force per unit charge
options.C: Charge per unit energy
options.D: Energy per unit time

questions.question_text: What physical role does the Boltzmann constant play, as described in this chapter?

options.A: It converts electric field into electric potential
options.B: It converts frequency into photon energy
options.C: It relates absolute temperature to the average thermal energy of particles
options.D: It relates electric charge to electric current

questions.question_text: What does the divergence of a vector field measure at a point?

options.A: The field's rotational tendency around the point
options.B: The net outward flow of the field per unit volume at the point
options.C: The direction of steepest increase of a scalar quantity
options.D: The magnitude of the field at that exact point only

questions.question_text: Two point charges are separated by distance r. If that distance is tripled while the charges stay the same, what happens to the electrostatic force between them, according to Coulomb's Law?

options.A: It becomes 1/3 of its original value
options.B: It becomes 3 times its original value
options.C: It stays the same
options.D: It becomes 1/9 of its original value

questions.question_text: Why is the electric field considered a more general description of electrostatic influence than the electrostatic force from Coulomb's Law?

options.A: The electric field is defined independent of any particular test charge, describing a property of space itself
options.B: The electric field only exists between two specific point charges
options.C: The electric field depends on the mass of the source charge
options.D: The electric field is a scalar quantity, unlike force

questions.question_text: According to Euler's formula introduced in this chapter, how is the complex exponential e^(i*theta) related to trigonometric functions?

options.A: e^(i*theta) equals sin theta divided by cos theta
options.B: e^(i*theta) equals cos theta plus i sin theta
options.C: e^(i*theta) equals cos theta minus sin theta
options.D: e^(i*theta) equals the magnitude of a complex number only

questions.question_text: How does the electric field relate to the electric potential via the gradient, as presented in this chapter?

options.A: The electric field equals the positive gradient of the potential
options.B: The electric field equals the curl of the potential
options.C: The electric field equals the negative gradient of the potential
options.D: The electric field equals the divergence of the potential

questions.question_text: A photon's wavelength is decreased while the speed of light stays constant. Based on E = hc/lambda, what happens to its energy?

options.A: The photon's energy decreases
options.B: The photon's energy stays exactly the same
options.C: The photon's energy becomes zero
options.D: The photon's energy increases

questions.question_text: Given the potential V(x,y,z) = 3x^2y + 2z, what is the partial derivative of V with respect to x?

options.A: 6xy
options.C: 6x

questions.question_text: A spherical Gaussian surface encloses a fixed point charge. If the radius of the sphere is doubled while the enclosed charge stays the same, what does Gauss's Law say happens to the total electric flux through the surface?

options.A: The flux quadruples
options.B: The flux is cut in half
options.C: The flux stays exactly the same
options.D: The flux drops to zero

questions.question_text: In this chapter's notation, what distinguishes a vector quantity like force from a scalar quantity like energy?

options.A: A vector has both magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only
options.B: A vector is always negative; a scalar is always positive
options.C: A vector can only describe electric quantities; a scalar cannot
options.D: A vector has magnitude only; a scalar has both magnitude and direction

questions.question_text: What does the curl of the static electric field equal, according to this chapter?

options.A: The charge density divided by permittivity
options.B: The electric flux through a closed surface
options.C: The gradient of the electric potential
options.D: Zero

questions.question_text: How is electric flux through a flat surface in a uniform field defined in this chapter?

options.A: The charge enclosed divided by the surface area
options.B: The field's component perpendicular to the surface, multiplied by the area
options.C: The field's component parallel to the surface, multiplied by the area
options.D: The total charge on the surface

questions.question_text: Why is the permittivity of free space, epsilon-0, classified as a fundamental physical constant rather than a property specific to one experiment?

options.A: Because its value changes depending on which material is being tested
options.B: Because it is measured in volts rather than farads per meter
options.C: Because it is the same fixed numerical value in every calculation involving electrostatics in a vacuum
options.D: Because it only applies inside semiconductor crystals

questions.question_text: A crystal has a uniform temperature and exchanges no net energy with its surroundings, but a second sample of the same material has hot and cold regions. Which sample is in thermal equilibrium, and why?

options.A: The first sample, because it has a single well-defined temperature and no net energy exchange with its surroundings
options.B: The second sample, because temperature differences drive useful energy flow
options.C: Neither sample, because thermal equilibrium requires an applied voltage
options.D: Both samples, because thermal equilibrium only depends on total energy, not its distribution

questions.question_text: If two like-signed point charges are moved closer together, what happens to their electrostatic potential energy, based on U = q_test V(r)?

options.A: It decreases
options.B: It becomes negative
options.C: It remains exactly zero
options.D: It increases

questions.question_text: Using V = V_T ln(I/I0 + 1), find V (in volts) when I = 99 I0 and V_T = 0.0259 V.

A charged particle is released from rest near a fixed point charge of the same sign and moves away under the resulting repulsive force. Which statement best explains the underlying reason its kinetic energy increases while its electrostatic potential energy decreases?

options.A: Total charge is being converted into mass as the particle moves
options.B: The particle is gaining energy from an external battery not described in the scenario
options.C: Conservation of mechanical energy requires that a decrease in potential energy appear as an equal increase in kinetic energy, since no external force removes energy from the system
options.D: Kinetic and potential energy are independent quantities with no required relationship
